Artificial intelligence (AI) has become the biggest story, the central story, perhaps the only story that matters to the stock market right now. But many investors are getting anxious.

The past few months have been bad for AI stocks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 officially entered a correction (a 10% or more decline), dropping 11.3% since Oct. 6 before gaining today. That's more than halfway to a bear market (a 20% or more decline).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Some major tech names that have been driving the AI trade, such as Nvidia, CoreWeave, Tesla, Oracle, and Palantir, have seen significant share price declines over the past year.

NVDA data by YCharts

Does this mean that AI stocks are "over" and it's time to move your money to bonds or cash? Not necessarily. There are a few possible future paths for what might happen next with AI stocks and the broader stock market.

AI executives have made some incredibly lofty predictions about what their technology might do in the future. We've heard bold claims that AI will boost U.S. GDP by 50% in just four years, but also that it will replace most entry-level white-collar jobs, or even be responsible for the extinction of mankind. I'm skeptical about these most extreme scenarios.

At the other extreme, some AI skeptics believe the technology is overrated, overpriced, and unlikely to deliver meaningful gains in productivity or economic growth. I feel like this is unlikely to be true for too long. Companies across industries are experimenting with AI to improve their processes, save time, and reduce costs. Are we really supposed to believe that all that effort will amount to nothing, that AI is just going to "go away"? I doubt that.

Instead, I think it's more likely that we find a happier middle ground on the future of AI.

Let's take a big-picture look at the future of AI stocks -- with optimistic (bull case), pessimistic (bear case), and middle-ground (base case) scenarios. And let's see how you could position your investments based on which outcome you think is most likely.

Image source: Getty Images.
Bull case: Today's AI stock winners keep winning

AI doesn't destroy human civilization or take all the jobs. Instead, it delivers game-changing productivity growth. Good news comes out about a highly popular, profitable new AI product that's a game changer, like Google search was in 1999 or the iPhone in 2007. Or AI gets cheaper to build. (Or both.)

One Investor Says Anthropic Would Cost "Less Than Palantir on Sales." That's a Problem for Palantir ©@dotshock via Canva, @dotshock via Canva
Key Takeaways

Anthropic set its IPO range at $70 to $78 a share. One investor on Reddit works that out to 35x to 39x trailing sales, compared with 53x for Palantir.

An AI company that's growing faster and listing at a lower sales multiple than Palantir makes Palantir's premium harder to defend.

Analysts expect Palantir's revenue growth to slow from about 91% this year to 53% in 2027. Anthropic's first-half revenue was about 14 times what it made a year earlier.

Palantir is profitable and Anthropic isn't yet. Palantir's first 2027 guidance, expected in early February, is the next test.

Anthropic set its IPO price range this week, and the math is awkward for Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ).

The AI lab will offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece, according to its updated filing. It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT next week. A poster on Reddit's r/ValueInvesting ran the numbers and summed it up like this:

"At its IPO range, Anthropic would cost less than Palantir on sales but nearly 3x Nvidia."

The poster puts Anthropic at 35x to 39x trailing sales, compared with 53x for Palantir and 13x for Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ). For Palantir shareholders, the top of that list is an uncomfortable place to sit.

Investors will make that comparison, too. On CNBC's Squawk Pod, a host argued that a lower price for Anthropic pulls valuations down across AI. Plexo Capital's Lo Toney answered that the listing "does put some pressure on those other companies," since investors are going to "use Anthropic as a benchmark." He was talking about private labs like OpenAI, but Palantir's shareholders get the same benchmark next week.

TIKR tracks 33 analysts on Palantir. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Palantir, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Palantir's Analyst Ratings

Palantir's premium is built on growth

Palantir's business is still firing. Third-quarter revenue rose 96% to $2.31 billion, and the company raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $8.53 billion. Even so, the stock is down 19% from its record close on Oct. 9. Part of the reason is that the value of new contracts it signed grew just 6% to $2.92 billion in the quarter, after 49% growth in the second quarter. Management blamed shorter contracts.

Analysts expect Palantir's revenue growth to slow from here:

Palantir Technologies (PLTR): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That's about 91% growth this year, then 53% in 2027 and 47% in 2028. Those are still terrific numbers, but they're a long way from the pace investors have been paying for.

The sale followed Palantir's third-quarter results, which exceeded headline analyst estimates but included slower growth in measures tied to future contracts. Total contract value growth eased to 6% from 49%, while growth in U.S. commercial contract value slowed to 11% from 153% in the previous period.

Those figures could draw investor attention because contract activity offers an indication of potential future revenue. The slowdown may complicate the outlook for a stock whose valuation reflects high expectations for continued expansion.

Direxion's Ryan Lee said Palantir entered earnings priced to perfection, pointing to the pressure created by elevated expectations. ARK's disclosed sale does not establish its investment rationale, but it adds to the focus on whether Palantir can sustain customer commitments and convert demand into future growth.

title: Midterm Meltdowns: 3 Top Tech Stocks Down Big Since the Election Results
detail:
Midterm Meltdowns: 3 Top Tech Stocks Down Big Since the Election Results
David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 11:22 AM MST 5 min read
NVDA
MU
PLTR
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Last week, the midterm elections shook up the markets. Many stocks have been falling since the news hit that the Democratic Party would be taking control of Congress. It's created uncertainty about how strong demand will be for data centers and whether there will be a slowdown in the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out that's been a boom for many tech businesses.

Three top tech stocks that have been falling sharply of late include Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU), and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR). Are these stocks worth buying on the dip?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia

A slowdown in AI spending could make Nvidia one of the most vulnerable stocks to own, as its AI chips are seen as essential for many companies investing in the latest opportunities in tech. Just prior to the midterms, Nvidia's stock was trading at over $206. But on Tuesday, it fell to below $170 -- a level it hasn't been at since March.

Nvidia's problems, however, aren't all due to the midterms. CEO Jensen Huang has been making news for all the wrong reasons of late, reportedly being involved in a romantic relationship with a Chinese spy. The company has launched its own investigation, and it begs the question of whether Huang will stay on as CEO.

There are now tremendous question marks around Nvidia, but ultimately, none of the recent developments likely change any of the company's impressive fundamentals. As long as there isn't a full-blown reduction in AI spending, which doesn't appear probable at this stage, the company is likely going to generate strong growth for the foreseeable future.

At just 21 times trailing earnings, Nvidia's looking like a bargain buy, and the stock may be too good to pass up at its current valuation.

Micron

Micron's stock was trading at over $855 on the eve of the midterms, and last week it fell below $700. While it's bounced back from those lows, it's still not far from those levels now.

In Micron's case, it's a much riskier stock to own than Nvidia, simply because so much of the bull case hinges on there being a continued shortage of memory and storage products. If there are any signs of that coming to an end, such as slowing demand for AI-related infrastructure, Micron's impressive growth could quickly stall, and the stock may be due for a deeper decline.
